title: Principles of Natural Justice — Nemo Judex In Causa Sua (Rule against Bias: Pecuniary, Personal, Subject-Matter)

content.overview: Nemo judex in causa sua is the natural-justice rule that a decision-maker must not sit on a matter in which they have a legally relevant interest or bias. Indian administrative law recognises pecuniary bias, personal bias and other forms of subject-matter or official bias that create a real likelihood of prejudice. The rule is applied in the context of the governing statute, the nature of the power and the consequences for the affected person.
content.glance: Ask whether the decision-maker had a pecuniary, personal or other relevant interest in the outcome, whether a fair-minded observer would find a real likelihood of bias, and whether the governing scheme or necessity provides a lawful exception.
content.study:
Core rule: a person should not be a judge in their own cause. In Indian administrative law the rule against bias protects the appearance and reality of impartial decision-making. It is closely linked to Articles 14 and 21 where administrative action affects rights, but its precise content is drawn from natural justice and the governing statutory scheme.

Pecuniary bias: Any direct financial interest in the outcome is ordinarily fatal. The law does not require proof of actual prejudice once a real pecuniary interest is shown.

Personal bias: Friendship, hostility, professional rivalry, family relationship or prior involvement that creates a real likelihood of bias may disqualify the decision-maker. The test is objective: whether a fair-minded and informed observer would conclude that there was a real possibility of bias.

Official / subject-matter bias: Participation by a person who has already taken a fixed view, or who combines the roles of investigator and adjudicator in a way that prevents an open mind, may also attract the rule. The analysis is fact-sensitive and turns on the statutory allocation of functions.

Exceptions and necessity: Bias may be displaced only where the statute clearly authorises the decision-maker despite the interest, or where the doctrine of necessity leaves no other competent forum. Convenience or administrative preference is not itself an exception.

Judicial review: Breach of the rule against bias is ordinarily treated as a jurisdictional or procedural defect. Relief is typically quashing and remittal to an unbiased decision-maker where possible. The court does not automatically substitute its own decision on the merits.

Current-law framing: Ground the analysis in the Constitution and the specific Act or rules creating the administrative power. Do not treat the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 as the source of the bias rule; evidence provisions apply only when proof or authenticity of material is actually in issue.

sections.heading: Meaning, Purpose and Constitutional Setting
sections.body: Nemo judex in causa sua means that no one should be a judge in their own cause. The purpose is to secure impartiality and public confidence in administrative decision-making. Articles 14 and 21 may inform constitutional review where the decision affects equality or personal liberty, but the bias inquiry itself is rooted in natural justice and the governing statutory framework.

sections.heading: Pecuniary Bias
sections.body: A direct pecuniary interest in the outcome ordinarily disqualifies the decision-maker. The existence of the interest is enough; the challenger need not prove that the interest actually altered the result. Indirect or remote financial interests require careful factual assessment of whether a real likelihood of bias arises.

sections.heading: Personal and Official Bias
sections.body: Personal bias covers relationships, prior hostility or favour, and other associations that create a real likelihood of prejudice. Official or subject-matter bias arises where the same person has already formed a concluded view or combines incompatible functions (for example investigator and adjudicator) so that an open mind cannot reasonably be expected. The test is objective and fact-sensitive.

sections.heading: Exceptions, Waiver and Necessity
sections.body: A statutory scheme may expressly or by necessary implication permit a decision-maker who would otherwise be biased. The doctrine of necessity may also justify decision-making where no other competent authority exists. Waiver by the affected person after full disclosure can sometimes cure the objection. None of these exceptions is automatic; each must be justified on the record.

sections.heading: Judicial Review and Relief
sections.body: A reviewing court asks whether a fair-minded observer would conclude that there was a real possibility of bias, having regard to the statutory scheme and the facts. If the defect is material, the ordinary remedy is to quash the decision and remit it to an unbiased decision-maker. The court should identify the precise form of bias and avoid treating every connection as automatically fatal.

examples.title: Pecuniary interest of the decision-maker
examples.body: A selection committee member stands to gain financially if a particular candidate is chosen. The issue is whether the direct pecuniary interest creates an automatic disqualification. The analysis should identify the statutory selection power, the nature of the financial interest, and whether any necessity or statutory exception applies.

examples.title: Prior concluded view
examples.body: An officer who has already recommended disciplinary action later sits as the inquiring authority on the same charges. The issue is whether the prior role created a real likelihood of bias or combined incompatible functions so that an open mind could not reasonably be expected.

examples.title: Necessity where no alternative forum exists
examples.body: A statutory body is the only authority competent to decide a dispute, yet one member has a personal connection to a party. The analysis must test whether the doctrine of necessity permits the body to act, whether the interested member can recuse, and what residual safeguards remain.

hypotheticals.question: A selection board includes a person who is a close relative of one of the shortlisted candidates. What should be examined?
hypotheticals.analysis: Identify the statutory composition of the board; determine the nature of the relationship; apply the real-likelihood-of-bias test from the standpoint of a fair-minded observer; consider whether the interested member can recuse and whether necessity or waiver applies; then decide the appropriate judicial-review remedy.

hypotheticals.question: Is every prior professional association between the decision-maker and a party fatal?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. First identify the precise connection and the statutory role. Determine whether a fair-minded observer would conclude that there was a real possibility of bias. Distinguish ordinary professional acquaintance from a relationship that creates a closed mind or personal interest in the outcome.

distinctions.title: Nemo judex vs audi alteram partem
distinctions.left: Nemo judex concerns impartiality of the decision-maker.
distinctions.right: Audi alteram partem concerns the affected person's opportunity to know and answer the case.

rows.right: Was a meaningful opportunity to be heard provided?

rows.left: Pecuniary, personal or other legally relevant bias.
rows.right: Defective notice, withheld material or no meaningful opportunity to respond.

distinctions.title: Nemo judex vs duty to give reasons
distinctions.left: Bias concerns the identity and impartiality of the decision-maker.
distinctions.right: Reasoned decision-making concerns explaining the basis of the decision where reasons are legally required.

rows.left: Who decides and whether they can be trusted to decide fairly.
rows.right: Whether the decision itself discloses a lawful and intelligible basis.

rows.left: Usually quashing and remittal to an unbiased decision-maker.
rows.right: May require a fresh reasoned order or fuller reasons.

misconceptions.trap: Any prior contact between the decision-maker and a party automatically voids the decision.
misconceptions.correction: The test is whether a fair-minded observer would find a real likelihood of bias; ordinary professional contact is not automatically fatal.

misconceptions.trap: The challenger must prove that the bias actually changed the result.
misconceptions.correction: For direct pecuniary interest the interest itself ordinarily suffices; for other forms the real-likelihood standard applies without requiring proof of actual persuasion.

misconceptions.trap: BSA provisions create the rule against bias.
misconceptions.correction: The bias rule arises from natural justice and the governing statutory scheme; evidence law is relevant only to evidentiary questions.

cases.name: A.K. Kraipak v Union of India
cases.facts: A selection process for public office involved participation by a person who had an interest in the outcome.
cases.issue: Whether natural justice, including the rule against bias, applied to the selection process and whether the interest invalidated the decision.
cases.ratioDecidendi: The Court held that the aim of natural justice is to prevent miscarriage of justice and that the administrative/quasi-judicial label does not by itself defeat the requirement of fairness where the facts show a relevant conflict.
cases.holding: The selection was invalidated on the facts because of the relevant conflict and lack of impartiality.
cases.relevance: Leading authority on the application of the rule against bias to administrative selection processes.

cases.name: Maneka Gandhi v Union of India
cases.facts: The case concerned procedural fairness applicable to an adverse administrative action affecting a fundamental right.
cases.issue: Whether the procedure affecting the person's right could be treated as fair merely because a statutory procedure existed.
cases.ratioDecidendi: The Court treated fairness and reasonableness as relevant to procedure affecting Article 21 interests.
cases.holding: The passport impounding action was examined against constitutional procedural fairness.
cases.relevance: Foundational authority linking fair procedure to constitutional guarantees; relevant context for bias challenges that engage fundamental rights.

cases.name: Swadeshi Cotton Mills v Union of India
cases.facts: The case concerned takeover action and the applicability of natural justice before an adverse administrative decision.
cases.issue: Whether the hearing requirement was excluded by the statutory scheme and urgency.
cases.ratioDecidendi: The Court examined the statutory context and circumstances to determine how natural justice operated.
cases.holding: Natural justice was not treated as automatically excluded merely by the existence of statutory power or claimed urgency.
cases.relevance: Useful comparative authority on the interaction between statutory scheme, urgency and natural-justice requirements that often appear alongside bias challenges.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a bias challenge be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Identify the statutory source and the decision-maker. II. State the alleged form of bias (pecuniary, personal or official/subject-matter). III. Apply the real-likelihood test from the standpoint of a fair-minded observer. IV. Test any statutory exception, necessity or waiver. V. Identify the appropriate judicial-review remedy (ordinarily quashing and remittal).

questionsAndAnswers.question: What should written submissions on nemo judex contain?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Set out the governing power and material facts; identify the precise form of bias and the decision-maker's interest or prior role; apply the real-likelihood standard; answer the authority's reliance on necessity, statutory composition or waiver; distinguish bias from mere prior professional contact; and seek only the relief supported by the governing law and record.

bareActPointers: Constitution of India — Articles 14, 21 and 226 where applicable
The specific Act, rules and delegated legislation creating the administrative power and constituting the decision-maker
Use BSA 2023 only where an actual evidentiary issue arises
examTips: Define nemo judex and immediately state the real-likelihood-of-bias test.
Separate pecuniary, personal and official/subject-matter bias as distinct checkpoints.
Do not treat every prior association as automatically fatal.
State the statutory source of power and composition of the decision-maker before discussing the bias challenge.
Conclude with the precise judicial-review remedy rather than an automatic nullity claim.
